newsitem.title: USA: DLJ, Goldman split over 1997 U.S. economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: DLJ, Goldman split over 1997 U.S. economic outlook.

text.p: Two prominent economists presented polar opposite 1997 forecasts for the U.S. economy at a mortgage banking conference Thursday.

Elliot Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said investors should expect monetary stimulus and declining interest rates this year. But William Dudley, managing director and head of U.S. economic research at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc, warned of above-trend growth and rising inflation.
Both economists addressed a Mortgage Bankers Association of America (MBA) conference here.
Platt said an expected swift slowdown in Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth underpins his projection of successive Federal Reserve interest rate cuts.
"We are anticipating a very sharp, non-recessionary slowdown in economic growth," said Platt, who projected output would rise only about 1.0 percent in 1997.
Demand for U.S. products, from both domestic consumers and foreign trading partners, should be flat to down this year, detracting from economic output, he said.

Growth falling from a fourth-quarter 1996 rate of between 3.0 to 4.0 percent should prompt the Federal Reserve to make successive cuts in the federal funds target rate, Platt said. The key short-term rate should decline to about 4.0 percent from its current 5.25 percent by yearend, he added.
Consequently, Platt forecast the bellwether 30-year bond yield would fall to about 5.5 percent by yearend from its current 6.78 percent.

Goldman's Dudley countered that growth may not slow on its own, as Platt had projected. Instead, he said, speedy growth would accelerate inflation and push the Fed toward a series of credit tightenings, setting off a rise in long-term rates.
Consumer spending, the largest component of GDP, seems to be quite healthy as 1997 begins, he said. Incomes are rising faster than spending, and consumer confidence has risen steadily, he said.
Annual GDP should be up about 2.9 percent in 1997, compared with a projected 2.4 percent gain in 1996, Dudley said.
At the same time, the unemployment rate should continue to drop further beneath the widely perceived Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment (NAIRU), Dudley said.

Wage inflation could be gathering steam because the unemployment rate has hovered below 5.5 percent for a few months, he said. "If there's a risk in 1997, it's that inflation rates go up, not down," Dudley said.
"We're going to end up with more monetary tightening than is generally anticipated" thanks to the pickup in inflation, the economist said.
Dudley projected about 100 basis points of tightening in 1997, coupled with a rising bond yield to about 7.4 percent.
David Lereah, chief economist at the MBA and the moderator of the Platt-Dudley discussion, said the economy "appears to be at a crossroads."
He said most of the conference audience would prefer to average the views of Dudley and Platt, since interest rates are at comfortable levels for mortgage bankers.
